title: The little scroll (Revelation 10)
hookLine: sweet as honey in the mouth, bitter in the stomach

lines: ONE FOOT ON THE SEA, ONE ON THE LAND.
cards: An angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, a rainbow over his head. He plants his right foot on the sea and his left on the land, and cries out like a lion roaring. Seven thunders answer.
John reaches to write down what they said, and a voice stops him: seal it up, and don't write it. So there are words in Revelation that Revelation keeps to itself.
Then a stranger order: go and take the little book open in the angel's hand. John asks for it. The angel hands it over and says: eat it.
That little book is today's word.

teach.h: SWEET IN THE MOUTH, BITTER INSIDE.
teach.b: The King James calls it a little book; the title here says little scroll. Either way, words small enough to hold in one hand.
First, the warning comes before the meal: "it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey."
John eats it anyway, and it's exactly as promised: "it was in my mouth sweet as honey: and as soon as I had eaten it, my belly was bitter." Second, John isn't alone.
Ezekiel was handed a scroll written with "lamentations, and mourning, and woe." He ate it too: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." A scroll full of grief, and it tasted like honey.
John's story leans on his. Third, why bitter?
The text doesn't say outright, so readers differ.
Some hear the calling: God's word is sweet to receive and heavy to carry, because the very next line is an order: "Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings."
Others hear the message itself: God's victory, and suffering still on the way, in one mouthful. Fourth, this isn't only a vision.

teach.h: TRUE THINGS CAN TASTE BOTH WAYS.
teach.b: Plenty of true things land this way. A diagnosis that finally explains the pain. An honest word from a friend.
A calling you know is yours, and know will cost you. Sweet to hear, and then it has to go all the way down.

how: Christians who read Revelation 10 alongside Ezekiel 2–3 often hear it as a picture of receiving God's word: preachers and readers speak of taking scripture in slowly, letting it become part of them, sweet and demanding at once.

games.why: John eats it all, and it's as promised: sweet as honey, then bitter. the next order follows at once: prophesy again.

practice: Let one truth come to mind that's good to know and hard to carry, about your life, your family or your work.

Don't fix it; hold it the way John held the little book, noticing where the sweet part is and where the hard part sits in your body. If you pray, bring both to God at once; if not, let both be true together for a minute.

wordCard.voice: The little scroll. The book John was told to eat in Revelation ten: sweet as honey in his mouth, bitter once it was inside him.

orig.note: Greek: a little book or little scroll, the thing John eats in Revelation 10.

carryVoice: Your line: sweet and bitter. From a knock at the door in Laodicea, through a Lamb, four riders and silence, this week ran to a book you eat. See you tomorrow.
